items.canonical_answer: Economic development is the sustained improvement in a country's living standards and material wellbeing, judged by income per head together with indicators such as life expectancy at birth, adult literacy, and access to clean water and electricity.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must name the improvement in living standards and the indicators that judge it - income per head plus life expectancy, literacy and access to services - because development covers more than output.

items.prompt: A survey of two neighbouring economies finds output per head of N$9 000 a year in one and N$90 000 in the other; in the first, a quarter of rural children do not finish primary school and one adult in ten cannot read. Analyse how a low level of development tends to hold back the next rise in development, tracing the chain for households, firms and the government.
items.canonical_answer: At N$9 000 a head, households spend most of their income on necessities, leaving little for schooling beyond what the state provides, and the government collects little tax, so its spending on schools, clinics and piped water stays thin. Each generation reaches working age with less education and worse health - here a quarter of rural children do not finish primary school - so output per worker stays low, and with it the income that would fund the next rise. The gap with the N$90 000 economy therefore tends to persist. Children carry the lost schooling into adulthood, households carry illness, firms face weaker skills, and the government lacks the revenue to break the chain.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the chain must open from the stated initial change - output per head of N$9 000 a year with a quarter of rural children not finishing primary school - not from a measure the prompt does not give.
Mechanism: the path from low income to weak schooling and health to low output per worker must be traced because each link is what carries the analysis.
Consequence: therefore the persistence of the gap - low development holding back its own improvement - must be the traced result.
For whom: the consequence must land on named parties - the children, the households, the firms and the government.

items.prompt: Two economies publish their figures for 2026. Country A: GDP per head N$40 000, life expectancy at birth 68 years, adults able to read 9 in 10, households with electricity 55%. Country B: GDP per head N$42 000, life expectancy at birth 76 years, adults able to read 99 in 100, households with electricity 98%. Using the figures, explain why the ranking of the two countries' development differs when income per head is replaced by the other indicators.
items.canonical_answer: B leads narrowly on GDP per head, N$42 000 against N$40 000, but widely elsewhere: life expectancy 76 years against 68, literacy 99 in 100 against 9 in 10, electricity 98% of households against 55%. Because development covers health, education and services as well as income, the real gap is wider than income shows: eight more years of life and 43 more homes in every hundred with power outweigh N$2 000 a head. So B is clearly more developed, though GDP per head puts the two close.
marking_guidance: Context: the data - the N$40 000 against N$42 000 GDP per head, the 68 against 76 years of life expectancy, the literacy and the electricity figures - must be used.
Reasoning: the link from each figure to what it says about living standards must be given, because a figure quoted without its meaning earns nothing.
Conclusion: therefore the answer must close on which country the indicators place ahead and why that ranking differs from the income measure.

items.prompt: Explain the features of a country's economic development that the indicators are chosen to measure.
items.canonical_answer: Development has four sides, each with its own indicator. Income, measured by GDP per head, sets the goods and services a person can command. Health, measured by life expectancy at birth, reflects the food, clinics and clean water available. Education, measured by adult literacy, sets what work a person can do. Access to services, measured by the share of households with electricity and piped water, shows what daily life can reach. A country counts as more developed where these are higher together, not on income by itself.
marking_guidance: Features: the elements required are income, health, education and access to services, each named with the indicator that measures it.
Characteristics: each feature must be explained - which side of living standards it covers and why it is measured - not merely listed.

items.prompt: Workers at a fish cannery in Walvis Bay each process 40 tins an hour with older equipment, while workers at a similar cannery in Spain each process 120 tins an hour with modern machinery. Analyse how this difference in productivity is likely to affect living standards in the two countries.
items.canonical_answer: Spanish workers process 120 / 40 = 3 times as many tins an hour, because they have more and better capital. Because each worker produces more, the Spanish firm can pay higher wages and still earn a profit, so workers' households have higher incomes. This causes higher spending and more tax revenue at the same tax rates, funding schools and clinics. Therefore living standards tend to be higher in Spain. In Namibia, lower productivity keeps wages and profits lower, limiting the saving that would pay for new machinery, so the gap may persist. Workers, firms and the government in both countries are affected.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the initial change - 120 against 40 tins an hour, a productivity gap caused by different equipment - must be stated.
Mechanism: because each worker produces more, this causes higher wages, profits and tax revenue in the more productive country.
Consequence: therefore living standards tend to be higher in Spain, while low productivity limits the saving and investment that would close the gap in Namibia.
For whom: workers, households, firms and the government must be named.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Country A's real GDP grows by 4% a year and its population by 3% a year. Country B's real GDP grows by 2% a year and its population by 0.2% a year. Using the figures, explain how this difference in population growth is likely to affect economic development in the two countries.
items.canonical_answer: Output per head grows by roughly 1% a year in A (4% less 3%) but by roughly 1.8% in B (2% less 0.2%), so B's living standards rise faster although A's output grows faster. In A, fast population growth means more young dependants, so more income goes on schools, food and clinics and less is saved and invested. In B, slow population growth lets more of the extra output reach each person. So faster population growth tends to hold back development unless the extra people find productive work.
marking_guidance: Context: the figures must anchor the answer - output growth of 4% against 2%, population growth of 3% against 0.2%, and the resulting growth in output per head of about 1% against 1.8%.
Reasoning: because extra output is shared among more people, and because young dependants absorb income that could be saved and invested, the link from population growth to development must be given.
Conclusion: therefore the answer must close on faster population growth holding back development in A, with the condition that the extra people do not find productive work.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Define the primary sector of an economy.
items.canonical_answer: The primary sector is the part of an economy that extracts natural resources from the land and sea, such as farming, fishing, forestry and mining.
marking_guidance: Precise definition: the meaning must name the extraction of natural resources, with an example such as farming, fishing or mining; describing manufacturing or services defines the secondary or tertiary sector instead.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: In Country L, 65% of workers are in farming, mostly on small family plots; in Country H, 3% are in farming and 78% in services. Analyse how this difference in the size of the sectors is likely to cause a difference in economic development between the two countries.
items.canonical_answer: Country L has 65% of workers in farming against 3% in H. Because small family plots use little capital, output per farm worker tends to be low, so with 65% of the workforce there, L's income per head is low. This causes low saving and tax revenue, so less is spent on schools, clinics and machinery. In H, 78% work in services and 19% in industry, where capital and skills make output per worker higher and support higher wages. Therefore H tends to be more developed. L's households also face income swings with weather and crop prices, and L's government has a small tax base.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the initial difference - 65% of L's workers in farming against 3% in H, with 78% of H's in services - must be stated.
Mechanism: because small farms use little capital, this causes low output per worker and low income in L, while services and industry raise output per worker in H.
Consequence: therefore H tends to be more developed, and L's income is lower and less stable.
For whom: households, workers and the government must be named.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Explain why low saving can hold back economic development in a low-income country.
items.canonical_answer: Where income is low, households spend most of it on necessities, so little is saved. Because banks lend out what is saved, low saving leaves few funds for firms to borrow for machinery, buildings and new businesses, so investment is low. With little new capital, productivity grows slowly, so incomes stay low, which keeps saving low again: a cycle. Investment from abroad or by the government can make up part of the gap.
marking_guidance: Reason: because low income is spent on necessities, saving is low, so banks have few funds to lend for investment.
Reason: because low investment means little new capital, productivity and income grow slowly, which keeps saving low in a cycle.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Country S and Country T each have GDP of US$50 billion. Country S saves and invests 30% of its GDP each year; Country T saves and invests 8%. Using the figures, explain how this difference is likely to affect economic development in the two countries.
items.canonical_answer: Each year S invests US$15 billion (30% of US$50 billion) against US$4 billion (8%) in T. Because investment adds machinery, roads and factories, S's capital stock grows faster, so its workers become more productive and incomes rise. Higher income lets S save more again, while T's low investment keeps productivity and income growing slowly. So S is likely to develop faster, provided its investment goes into capital that firms actually use.
marking_guidance: Context: the figures must anchor the answer - 30% against 8% of US$50 billion, or US$15 billion against US$4 billion a year.
Reasoning: because investment adds capital that raises productivity, the link from the investment gap to faster growth of income in S must be given.
Conclusion: therefore S is likely to develop faster, with the condition that the investment is productive.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: In Country V, malaria and poor access to clinics mean the average worker loses 20 working days a year to illness; in Country W, with clinics and clean water widely available, the figure is 5 days. Analyse how this difference in health care is likely to affect economic development in the two countries.
items.canonical_answer: Workers in V lose 20 - 5 = 15 more days a year to illness than in W. Because sick workers produce nothing, output per worker is lower in V, and households lose earnings while paying for treatment. This causes lower incomes, lower saving and less tax revenue, so V can afford fewer clinics and schools. Ill children also miss school, so the next generation's skills suffer. Therefore V tends to be less developed than W, with shorter life expectancy and lower income per head. Workers, households, firms and V's government all bear the cost.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the initial difference - 20 against 5 working days lost to illness, from differences in health care - must be stated.
Mechanism: because sick workers produce nothing and households pay for treatment, this causes lower output, earnings, saving and tax revenue in V.
Consequence: therefore V tends to be less developed, with lower income per head and shorter lives.
For whom: workers, households, firms and the government must be named.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Explain why differences in education can cause differences in economic development between countries.
items.canonical_answer: Education gives workers skills - reading, calculating, using technology - so each worker can produce more, and productivity and wages are higher. A well-educated workforce also attracts firms making higher-value goods and services, such as electronics or banking, raising income further. Where many children leave school early, workers have fewer skills, firms find few qualified staff, and the country tends to stay in low-paid farming and simple manufacturing, so income per head and development stay lower.
marking_guidance: Reason: because education raises skills, productivity and wages are higher in better-educated countries.
Reason: because skilled workforces attract higher-value firms, while early school-leaving leaves few qualified workers, income per head and development differ.

items.prompt:
Eight questions in the style of Paper 1. Choose one option for each.

1. Economic development is best defined as the sustained improvement in:
A  the government's budget position
B  living standards, judged by income and other indicators
C  the total value of a country's exports
D  the size of a country's population

2. GDP per head is calculated by dividing:
A  total output by the population
B  the population by total output
C  total output by the number of workers
D  tax revenue by the population

3. A country's total output is N$300 billion and its population is 3 million people. GDP per head is:
A  N$100 000
B  N$1 000 000
C  N$100 000 000
D  N$10 000

4. Which indicator is used to judge the health side of development?
A  adult literacy
B  life expectancy at birth
C  GDP per head
D  the share of households with electricity

5. Two countries have similar GDP per head, but in one life expectancy at birth is 10 years longer. The longer-lived country is judged more developed because:
A  total output, not income per head, settles the comparison
B  health indicators count alongside income per head
C  a larger population counts as development by itself
D  life expectancy, not income, is the sole indicator

6. A low-income country tends to collect little tax revenue. This tends to hold back development because:
A  less can be spent on schooling, health and clean water, weakening the skills and health of workers
B  the population grows faster as a rule
C  exports tend to fall
D  output per head tends to rise

7. Which statement about GDP per head is correct?
A  it shows how income is shared within a country
B  it is an average, so it may sit high while many households stay poor
C  it measures total output rather than output per person
D  it records life expectancy alongside income

8. Which list contains indicators used together to judge development?
A  GDP per head, life expectancy at birth, adult literacy
B  total output, tax revenue, government spending
C  population, birth rate, death rate
D  exports, imports, the exchange rate
items.canonical_answer:
Key: 1 B, 2 A, 3 A, 4 B, 5 B, 6 A, 7 B, 8 A.
1. B is the definition; A confuses development with the fiscal position, C with trade performance, D with population change.
2. A is the formula; B reverses the division, C divides by workers instead of people, which measures output per worker, and D replaces output with government revenue.
3. N$300 billion ÷ 3 million people = N$100 000, so A; B drops the millions, C keeps them and drops the thousands, D divides by thirty million instead of three.
4. Life expectancy is the health indicator, so B; A measures education, C income, D services.
5. Development takes health into account alongside income, so B; A ranks by the wrong measure, C mistakes population size for development, D makes one indicator do the whole job.
6. Thin tax revenue thins the services that build skills and health, so A; B and C name changes the prompt does not give, D reverses the direction of the chain.
7. An average conceals its own spread, so B; A claims the average shows what sharing within the country looks like, C confuses per head with the total, D describes the indicator set rather than GDP per head.
8. The indicator set is income, health and education, so A; B lists public-finance totals, C lists population measures, which topic 5.3 owns, D lists trade measures.
marking_guidance: One mark per question; the key and the distractor explanations are the teaching back of the set.

Each distractor explanation names the specific misunderstanding it catches - the definition boundary, the reversed or mis-set division for GDP per head, and the average-versus-sharing reading of income.

Questions 3, 5 and 7 carry the topic's core discriminations, so their distractor explanations do the teaching: total output against output per head, income against the wider indicators, and an average against the living standards of the typical household.

facts: P01 covers the definition of economic development, the GDP per head formula and its calculation, the indicator set, and why GDP per head by itself can mislead

items.prompt:
A report for a regional development bank, 2027: "Country A produced total output of N$120 billion this year with a population of 4 million people. Country B, its neighbour, produced N$90 billion with 1.5 million people. In A, children born this year can expect 61 years of life and one adult in ten cannot read; in B, life expectancy is 74 years and two adults in a hundred cannot read. Just over half of A's households have electricity, against almost all of B's."

Table 1 - Country A and Country B
  total output: A N$120 billion, B N$90 billion
  population: A 4 million people, B 1.5 million people
  life expectancy at birth: A 61 years, B 74 years
  adults who cannot read: A 1 in 10, B 2 in 100
  households with electricity: A 55%, B 96%

(a) Calculate country A's GDP per head. [1]
(b) Identify from Table 1 two indicators, other than output, on which B leads A. [2]
(c) Explain why total output by itself may mislead when judging which country is more developed. [4]
(d) Analyse why the indicators in Table 1 tend to move together, using the data as evidence. [6]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) GDP per head = total output ÷ population = N$120 billion ÷ 4 million people = N$30 000 per head.
(b) Life expectancy at birth, where B's 74 years stand against A's 61 years, and adult literacy, where in B 2 adults in 100 cannot read against 1 in 10 in A.
(c) Total output puts A ahead - N$120 billion against N$90 billion - because A has the larger population. Because GDP per head divides output by population, A's N$120 billion spread across 4 million people gives N$30 000 per head, while B's smaller N$90 billion spread across 1.5 million people gives N$60 000 per head. This means the country producing less in total is the one whose people command twice as much each, so the total-output ranking puts the less developed country first. A comparison of development therefore ranks output per head, because population size, not living standards, is what decides the total.
(d) Where GDP per head is higher, the other indicators tend to be higher too, because income on both sides of the chain drives them. In the data, B's GDP per head of N$60 000 stands against A's N$30 000, and B leads on life expectancy at birth (74 years against 61 years), adult literacy (2 in 100 unable to read against 1 in 10) and electricity (96% of households against 55%). Higher income per head lets households buy better food, schooling and lighting, and it widens the tax base, so the government can fund clinics, teachers and power lines; each indicator is both a result of income and a cause of it, because literate, healthy workers raise output per head further. As a result, households in B live the longer, more literate, electrified lives; firms in B draw on healthier, better-read workers; A's government starts from a smaller revenue base to fund the same services. However, the link is not mechanical - a country whose income rests on a single mineral may report high GDP per head while its life expectancy and literacy trail behind, where the income is concentrated in few hands or spent little on services.
marking_guidance: Parts (a) and (b) are read from the data; the six-mark part must use the figures as evidence - the N$30 000 against N$60 000 of GDP per head, the 74 against 61 years, the electricity shares - not as analysis itself.
One mark per distinct linked statement in (c) and (d): a relationship, a reason or a named consequence counts where it is linked, not merely listed.
Part (d) is marked on expected relationship, then evidence, then analysis, then an exception; quoting figures without the relationship they support earns nothing.
For whom: the six-mark analysis must name the parties the differences land on - the households, the firms and the government of each country.

facts: Country A total output N$120 billion, population 4 million people
Country B total output N$90 billion, population 1.5 million people
life expectancy at birth: A 61 years, B 74 years
adults who cannot read: A 1 in 10, B 2 in 100

items.prompt:
A landlocked economy plans to move from output per head of N$8 000 towards its neighbours' N$40 000.
(a) Define the term economic development. [2]
(b) Explain, using the purpose of indicators, two reasons why GDP per head is used together with other indicators to judge development. [4]
(c) The government raises spending on primary schooling by a fifth of its education budget, funded from borrowing. Analyse the likely effects of this measure on the country's development. [6]
(d) Discuss whether a country whose total output is growing quickly should be classed as developed. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Economic development is the sustained improvement in a country's living standards, judged by income per head together with indicators such as life expectancy at birth, adult literacy and access to clean water and electricity.
(b) First reason: GDP per head is an average, so it may conceal how income is shared - where income is concentrated in a few hands, the typical household may live far below the average, and indicators such as life expectancy and literacy show what the average hides. Second reason: income does not record the non-material sides of living standards - health, education and services such as clean water and power - which development includes, so these are measured by their own indicators and read alongside income.
(c) The government adds a fifth of its education budget to primary schooling, funded from borrowing. Because more children complete primary school, this causes literacy among the next cohort of workers to rise; because literate workers tend to produce more in an hour, output per head tends to rise with it, and the wider tax base this brings lets later budgets fund clinics and power lines as well as schools. Therefore the country's development tends to improve on the education indicator first, then on income and the service indicators as the schooled cohorts reach work. Children gain the schooling, their future employers gain better-read workers, and the taxpayer carries the borrowing until the wider tax base arrives; where the borrowing squeezes clinic spending, the health indicators may move more slowly than the education ones.
(d) Why it might: growth in total output raises what households, firms and the government command, and where growth in output runs ahead of population growth, output per head rises, which is the income side of development; a government whose output is growing collects more revenue to extend schooling, clinics and power lines, so the other indicators may follow. Why it might not: total output can grow quickly while output per head barely moves, where population grows as fast; growth concentrated in one industry may leave most households and regions untouched, so literacy and life expectancy show little change; and development includes health, education and services that a total-output figure does not record at all. Judgement: on balance a country whose total output is growing quickly should be classed as developing rather than developed, because development is a level of living standards and not a speed of growth. The condition the judgement depends on: whether output per head and the wider indicators are rising with the total - where they are, the growth is delivering development; where population growth or concentration absorbs it, the total says little about how people live.
marking_guidance: Every part carries a model answer; part (d) is level-marked over three bands.
(a) rewards the precise meaning: sustained improvement in living standards, judged by income per head and the wider indicators.
(b) one mark per distinct reason with its link made: the average-versus-sharing point and the non-material point, each carried to why another indicator is needed.

(c) one mark per distinct linked statement from the starting point - a fifth of the education budget into primary schooling, funded from borrowing - through the mechanism to the consequence for named parties.

(d) the top band examines why it might and why it might not, reaches a judgement, and names the condition the judgement depends on - whether output per head and the wider indicators rise with the total.

facts: output per head now N$8 000, neighbours' level N$40 000
primary schooling spending raised by a fifth of the education budget, funded from borrowing

items.prompt: Plan an answer to: "Discuss whether GDP per head is the best measure of a country's economic development." Do not write the essay; produce the plan.
items.canonical_answer:
Case for (the income core): GDP per head measures what people can command, and it travels across borders, counted the same way for most countries each year.
Chain 1: GDP per head rises -> households command more goods and services -> living standards improve on the income side -> the other indicators tend to follow, because richer households buy food, schooling and lighting (for whom: households gain purchasing power; firms gain larger markets; the government gains revenue).
Case against (the average hides the spread): GDP per head is an average, so where income is concentrated the typical household may live far below it.
Chain 2: income concentrated in few hands -> the average stays high -> literacy and life expectancy for the many trail the average -> development is overstated (for whom: poorer households stay unserved; the government misreads its own progress).
Case against, second point (income is part of development, not the whole): health, education and services are sides of living standards income does not record.
Chain 3: clinic or clean water unreachable -> income buys less wellbeing -> the indicators diverge from income -> the single measure misranks countries (for whom: households carry illness and water-carrying whatever the average says).
Judgement: GDP per head is the best single starting measure, provided the others are read with it, because income carries the widest comparison across countries; the condition the judgement depends on is how income is shared and how far services reach - where either fails, the indicator set outranks the single measure.
marking_guidance: A plan, not an essay: the chains and the stated judgement are what is assessed.
Criterion: the decisive factor is whether the average reflects the typical household and whether services reach it.
Counterargument: the case against must appear - the average hiding the spread of income, and income not recording health, education and services.
Condition: the plan must end on what would change the judgement - how income is shared and how far services reach.
For whom: each chain names who gains and who is missed - households, firms, the government.
